name: Sjiagha-Jenimu / Syiagha-Yenimu
confidence_why: Drabbe 1950, the only first-hand description, says the prominence "lijkt veel op de Nederlandse klemtoon" and marks it with a grave accent without stating where it falls, and Voorhoeve 1975, summarizing Drabbe, likewise reports stress with no placement rule, so the record (stress present, placement undetermined) rests on one thin but unopposed source.

catalog_quote: [Drabbe 1950: 96] De toon, die op een syllabe valt, lijkt veel op de Nederlandse klemtoon; we geven hem aan met een accent-grave. ... [Voorhoeve 1975: 375] The only difference between the sound systems of Syiagha-Yenimu and Sawuy is the probable presence of a sixth vowel, ɛ, in Syiagha-Yenimu. Minor differences on the allophonic level may exist, but the very global phonetic description by Drabbe does not allow to go into details. Supra-segmentals: stress, but no rules of stress placement have been given.

new_statements.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Voorhoeve 1975, PL C-38, p. 375 (PDF page 31 of; page scan, viewed): sec. 2.6.2.2.6.2.2 'Syiagha-Yenimu' ends exactly "The only difference between the sound systems of Syiagha-Yenimu and Sawuy is the probable presence of a sixth vowel, ɛ, in Syiagha-Yenimu. Minor differences on the allophonic level may exist, but the very global phonetic description by Drabbe does not allow to go into details. Supra-segmentals: stress, but no rules of stress placement have been given." Verbatim. Same section: "There are two dialects, Syiagha, and Yenimu. The data presented below represent the Syiagha dialect.. Drabbe (1950a) published a grammatical sketch of Syiagha-Yenimu,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand only: Voorhoeve's survey, summarising Drabbe 1950a (the only description; data = Syiagha dialect), says the language has stress but that the primary source gives no rule for where it falls. No placement rule is available from any opened source. (For comparison, the same survey gives Aghu 'weak stress on the last syllable of monomorphemic words' and Sawuy 'last syllable usually carries the main stress', but says nothing of the kind for Syiagha-Yenimu.)
new_statements.exceptions: none; Wester 2014 (Table 3.2) reports only that in endocentric noun compounds the first (modifying) noun carries the stress, Shiaxa included, Yenimu lacking data.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level implied ('stress placement'); no discussion of citation forms vs phrases.
new_statements.identity_note: Voorhoeve 1975's data 'represent the Syiagha dialect' of Syiagha-Yenimu (= South Awyu, sout2941, also called Oser; Glottolog lists no dialect children but links Lexibank 'Syiagha' and 'Yenimu' wordlists). Drabbe 1950 covers both dialects; Yenimu is the less described. Not to be confused with Drabbe 1957 (Aghu, aghu1254), Drabbe 1947 (Pisa = Asue Awyu, unpublished KITLV ms.) or Drabbe 1959 (Kaeti/Wambon, Dumut).

new_statements.quote: De toon, die op een syllabe valt, lijkt veel op de Nederlandse klemtoon; we geven hem aan met een accent-grave. [p. 96] — In beide dialecten vinden we het parallel van het Nederlandse „kokosnoot", met de toon op het eerste woord, bv. Sj. ji ro „boomvrucht" [p. 97] — men merke op dat de toon valt op de tijdwijzer [Sj. praet. hesternum, p. 114] — de toon valt ook hier weer op de tijdwijzer [Sj. praet. distans, p. 115]
new_statements.translation: The tone that falls on a syllable much resembles Dutch stress; we mark it with a grave accent. [p. 96] — In both dialects we find the parallel of Dutch 'kokosnoot' [coconut], with the stress on the first word, e.g. Sj. ji ro 'tree fruit' [p. 97] — note that the stress falls on the tense marker [Sjiagha yesterday-past, p. 114] — here again the stress falls on the tense marker [Sjiagha distant past, p. 115]
new_statements.citation: Drabbe, Peter. 1950. Twee dialecten van de Awju-taal (met kaartje). Bijdragen tot de Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde 106(1): 92-147.
new_statements.locator: sec. 2 (Klanken), last sentence, p. 96 (p. 5); sec. 5 p. 97; secs. 40-41 pp. 114-115; sec. 42 p. 116; wordlist pp. 131-145
new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: (PDF p = printed p - 91). extracted text p.5 (printed p.96), last sentence of sec. 2: 'De toon, die op een syllabe valt, lijkt veel op de Nederlandse klemtoon; we geven hem aan met een accent-grave.' verbatim. p.6 (p.97) sec. 5: 'In beide dialecten vinden we. het parallel van het Nederlandse "kokosnoot", met de toon op het eerste woord, bv. Sj. ji ro "boomvrucht"' verbatim. p.23 (p.114) sec. 40, inside the Sj. paragraph (da-go-dewe..): 'men merke op dat de toon valt pp de tijdwijzer' (text has scanned 'pp' for 'op'); p.24 (p.115) sec. 41 Sj. praet. dist. mak: 'de toon valt ook hier weer op dé tijdwijzer' (scanned 'dé' for 'de'). The minor differences are text-layer scanned noise, not source…
new_statements.relation_note: Confirms the existing Voorhoeve 1975 second-hand statement (stress present, no placement rule given) at its primary source, and adds the compound-stress and tense-marker-stress facts and the sparse accent-marked wordlist; nothing yields a word-level placement rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress exists and is Dutch-like in quality; Drabbe marks it ad hoc with a grave accent and gives no rule for where it falls in simple words. The only positional statements are morphological: endocentric noun-noun compounds are stressed on the first member (Sj. ji ro), and in the Sjiagha yesterday-past and distant-past verb forms the stress sits on the tense marker (-gö-/-oghö-/-nggö-, -mak-). The wordlist (pp. 131-145) carries grave accents on 66 lines with no single position dominating (chèjba, fagè, bédó-midi, ajè, chosè).
new_statements.exceptions: Jénimu praet. distans with m+-verbs: the stem-final vowel is 'toonloos' (unstressed) and can be dropped in writing (émmafi from émé-, p. 115); Jénimu praet. historicum: 'de toon valt op de klinker vóór dr' (ati-dréfi, p. 116). The Pisa (P.) statements — 2pl imperative stressed on -ni (p. 123), prohibitive stressed on -de (p. 124), possessive order with 'omgekeerde toon' (p. 97) — concern Pisa, a different Awyu language, not sout2941.
new_statements.identity_note: Drabbe 1950 describes the Sjiagha (Sj.) dialect 'as spoken by the Aboghoj group at Gimikja' with Jénimu (J.) deviations noted, plus Pisa (P.), which is a different Awyu language (Wildeman/Kampong tributaries; the P. stress remarks on pp. 97, 123, 124 are not about sout2941). Glottolog sout2941 = South Awyu [aws]; per Lebold, Kriens & Susanto 2013 fn. 3 p. 4 and Appendix A, the old Ethnologue code Siagha-Yenimu [osr] was split into South Awyu [aws] (villages Konebi, Yeloba, Banamepe on the Bamgi = Yenimu and lower Digul, plus Korome) and Edera Awyu [awy]; Siagha is the old name of the Ia River, Yenimu of the Bamgi. Drabbe's Sjiagha/Jénimu data thus belong to South Awyu, though a share of the old osr area is now Edera Awyu.

Voorhoeve 1975 says it gives no stress-placement rule, but its klankleer and accent-marked wordlist need to be read first-hand; it is open access (CC-BY-NC) yet brill.com's WAF blocks our network and direct download, and the Internet Archive copy (snapshot 20200211230130 of the downloadpdf URL) is unreachable from here.
